pos: n. (a steep ascent or precipice; the pass of Ziz)
etymology: Old English clif, a steep rock face. The Hebrew behind the single Authorized Version occurrence means an ascent, and it names the narrow pass up from the Dead Sea by which the invading armies climbed toward Jehoshaphat.
biblical_def: To morrow go ye down against them: behold, they come up by the cliff of Ziz; and ye shall find them at the end of the brook, before the wilderness of Jeruel. The word arrives inside one of the most remarkable military instructions in Scripture. A vast company of Moab and Ammon and Mount Seir was coming against Judah; Jehoshaphat feared, proclaimed a fast, and prayed the prayer that ends, we have no might against this great company that cometh against us; neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee. The answer came through Jahaziel, and it named the map. God tells them the road the enemy will take and the place they will be found, and then tells them they will not fight: ye shall not need to fight in this battle: set yourselves, stand ye still, and see the salvation of the LORD with you. They went out singing, the ambushments were set against the invaders, and every man of the host was dead when Judah arrived. The cliff of Ziz is therefore one of those exact geographical details Scripture keeps, marking the place where a nation learned that the battle is the LORD's.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a steep bank; a precipice; in Scripture, the ascent of Ziz by which the invaders came up against Jehoshaphat.
webster_full: CLIFF, n. A steep bank; as the cliffs of Dover; a precipice.
ASCENT, n. The act of rising; the way by which one ascends; an eminence.
PRECIPICE, n. A steep descent of land; a headlong steep.
AMBUSHMENT, n. A lying in wait for the purpose of attacking by surprise.
DELIVERANCE, n. Release from captivity, slavery, oppression or any restraint.
scriptures: To morrow go ye down against them: behold, they come up by the cliff of Ziz; and ye shall find them at the end of the brook, before the wilderness of Jeruel.
O our God, wilt thou not judge them? for we have no might against this great company that cometh against us; neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee.

Ye shall not need to fight in this battle: set yourselves, stand ye still, and see the salvation of the LORD with you, O Judah and Jerusalem: fear not, nor be dismayed; to morrow go out against them: for the LORD will be with you.
Psa 61:2
From the end of the earth will I cry unto thee, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock that is higher than I.
corruption_summary: Prayer is treated as a way of generating resolve within the one praying rather than as an appeal to a God who acts in history; Jehoshaphat's prayer ends in ignorance and dependence, and the answer names a road on a map.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern account of prayer as a spiritual practice that centres the practitioner cannot survive 2 Chronicles 20. Jehoshaphat says outright that he has no might and does not know what to do, which is the opposite of resolve, and the answer he receives is external, specific, and factual: they will come by the cliff of Ziz, you will find them at the end of the brook, and you will not need to fight. Nothing in the chapter is about the king's inner state except its emptiness. Everything is about God's action, and the singers went out in front of the army because the outcome was settled before the march.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself, and the principle to recover is the plain objectivity of providence. God governs the roads armies take and the passes they climb. The verse that follows the deliverance is the one to keep: the fear of God was on all the kingdoms of those countries, when they had heard that the LORD fought against the enemies of Israel. Deliverance is for the glory of the Deliverer, and the singers had it right before the swords did.
roots_summary: Hebrew ma'aleh (H4608), an ascent or steep place, rendered cliff; nachal (H5158), a brook or wadi; midbar (H4057), a wilderness.
roots_lines: Hebrew ma'aleh (H4608) — an ascent, a steep place, a pass; the cliff of Ziz.
Hebrew nachal (H5158) — a torrent-bed, a brook, a wadi; the end of the brook.
Hebrew midbar (H4057) — a wilderness, a pasture-land; the wilderness of Jeruel.
Hebrew yeshuw'ah (H3444) — salvation, deliverance; see the salvation of the LORD.
Hebrew yatsab (H3320) — to set or station oneself, to stand firm; set yourselves, stand ye still.

“our eyes are upon thee” — the end of Jehoshaphat's prayer.
“lead me to the rock that is higher than I” — the rock as refuge rather than obstacle.

pos: n. (a rough broken rock; the eagle's nesting place)
etymology: From a Celtic root meaning rock. The Authorized Version uses it once, in the LORD's speech out of the whirlwind, where the eagle's choice of a nesting site is offered to Job as evidence that he did not design the world.
biblical_def: She dwelleth and abideth on the rock, upon the crag of the rock, and the strong place. The LORD is questioning Job out of the whirlwind, and the method is unusual. He does not explain the suffering. He conducts a tour of creation and asks, at every stop, whether Job arranged it: where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth; hast thou entered into the treasures of the snow; canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades; doth the eagle mount up at thy command, and make her nest on high. The crag is one detail in that tour, and its force is cumulative. A bird chooses an unreachable rock, sees the prey afar off, and feeds her young with blood, and no man taught her, and no man could. By the end Job says, I know that thou canst do every thing, and that no thought can be withholden from thee, and then lays his hand upon his mouth. The crag is also a warning where the same Hebrew figure recurs: Obadiah addresses Edom in the clefts of the rock, whose habitation is high, who saith in his heart, Who shall bring me down to the ground. The same height is safety for the eagle and self-deception for a proud nation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a steep rugged rock; a rough broken rock, or point of a rock; in Scripture, the eagle's stronghold in the LORD's speech to Job.
webster_full: CRAG, n. A steep rugged rock; a rough broken rock, or point of a rock.
EAGLE, n. A rapacious fowl of the genus Falco, remarkable for strength, swiftness and sight.
STRONGHOLD, n. A fastness; a fort; a fortified place; a place of security.
WHIRLWIND, n. A violent wind moving in a circle, or rather in a spiral form.
SOVEREIGNTY, n. Supreme power; supremacy; the possession of the highest power.
scriptures: She dwelleth and abideth on the rock, upon the crag of the rock, and the strong place.
Doth the eagle mount up at thy command, and make her nest on high?
Job 38:4
Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding.
Oba 1:3
The pride of thine heart hath deceived thee, thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock, whose habitation is high; that saith in his heart, Who shall bring me down to the ground?
corruption_summary: The answer God gives Job is treated as evasion, because it supplies no reason for the suffering; the book presents the tour of creation as the answer, addressed to what a creature is competent to judge.
corruption_paragraphs: Readers who come to Job for a theodicy and leave with a catalogue of ostriches and eagles often conclude that God changed the subject. He did not. The question under the whole book is whether Job is in a position to arraign the government of the world, and the tour answers it by exhibiting a thousand arrangements Job neither made nor understands, from the foundations of the earth to the crag where an eagle nests. If a man cannot account for the instincts of a bird, his confidence that he could have run the universe more justly is not a serious claim, and God treats it seriously enough to dismantle it item by item.

The pastoral edge is that Job is never called wicked. God defends him against the friends at the end and restores him. What is corrected is the creature's assumption of competence to sit in judgment on the Judge, and the correction leaves Job better off than the explanation would have: I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee. Obadiah shows the other outcome, where height is mistaken for security — the pride of thine heart hath deceived thee. The same rock holds an eagle safely and cannot hold a proud man at all.

pos: n. (a small inlet or bay of the sea)
etymology: From Old Norse kriki, a nook or bend. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Luke's account of Paul's shipwreck, of the inlet with a beach into which the sailors hoped to run the ship.
biblical_def: And when it was day, they knew not the land: but they discovered a certain creek with a shore, into the which they were minded, if it were possible, to thrust in the ship. Luke is writing as a man who was aboard, and the chapter is one of the most precise pieces of seamanship in ancient literature: soundings taken, anchors cast out of the stern, the boat cut loose, the wheat thrown into the sea, the rudder bands loosed, the mainsail hoisted to the wind. And running through all of it is an angel's promise Paul had already announced to the ship: fear not, Paul; thou must be brought before Caesar, and lo, God hath given thee all them that sail with thee. Paul's comment on that promise is the doctrine of the chapter: be of good cheer: for I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me. Yet when the sailors tried to flee, Paul said, except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved. The promised end did not suspend the means. The creek is where the means and the promise meet: they ran the ship aground, it broke, and they escaped all safe to land.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a small inlet, bay or cove; a recess in the shore of the sea; in Scripture, the inlet where Paul's ship was run aground.
webster_full: CREEK, n. A small inlet, bay or cove; a recess in the shore of the sea, or of a river.
SHORE, n. The coast or land adjacent to the ocean or sea, or to a large lake or river.
SHIPWRECK, n. The destruction of a ship or vessel by being cast ashore or broken by rocks.
MEANS, n. That which is used to effect an object; the instrument or agency.
PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.
scriptures: And when it was day, they knew not the land: but they discovered a certain creek with a shore, into the which they were minded, if it were possible, to thrust in the ship.
Wherefore, sirs, be of good cheer: for I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me.
And the rest, some on boards, and some on broken pieces of the ship. And so it came to pass, that they escaped all safe to land.
He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still.
corruption_summary: Trust in God's promise is set against the diligent use of ordinary means, as though faith made seamanship unnecessary; Acts 27 has Paul announcing the promise and insisting the crew stay aboard in the same night.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors share this chapter as their graveyard. The first is the fatalism that reasons from a certain outcome to the irrelevance of action — if God has given Paul all them that sail with him, let the sailors go. Paul's answer to the centurion is flat: except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved. The decree includes the means. The second error is the practical atheism that runs the ship well and never mentions God, which the crew had been doing for fourteen days while neither sun nor stars appeared and all hope was taken away. Luke gives us both corrected in one man on one deck, taking bread and giving thanks to God in the presence of them all, and then telling everyone to eat because it is for their health.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, and the principle to recover is the Reformed doctrine of concurrence: God ordains the end and the means together, so that prayer, prudence, medicine, and soundings are not rivals to providence but its instruments. Psalm 107 is the seaman's psalm and says both halves — they cry unto the LORD in their trouble, and he maketh the storm a calm.
roots_summary: Greek kolpos (G2859), a bay or bosom, rendered creek; aigialos (G123), a beach or shore; diasozo (G1295), to bring safely through.
roots_lines: Greek kolpos (G2859) — a bosom, a bay or creek; the inlet of Acts 27:39.
Greek aigialos (G123) — a beach, a shore; a creek with a shore.
Greek diasozo (G1295) — to save thoroughly, to bring safe through; they escaped all safe to land.
Greek euthumeo (G2114) — to be of good cheer; Paul's word to the ship.
Greek pisteuo (G4100) — to believe, to trust; I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me.
usage: “they discovered a certain creek with a shore” — the single occurrence.
“I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me” — the doctrine of the chapter.
“they escaped all safe to land” — the promise kept, through the means.

pos: n. (a valley; in the Authorized Version, the king's dale)
etymology: Old English dael, a valley. The Authorized Version uses it twice, both times in the phrase the king's dale, and the two occurrences stand at opposite ends of the story of Israel's kings.
biblical_def: The first mention is Abram's: the king of Sodom went out to meet him after his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer, at the valley of Shaveh, which is the king's dale. There Melchizedek brought forth bread and wine and blessed him, and Abram gave him tithes of all and refused so much as a thread or a shoelatchet from the king of Sodom. The second is Absalom's, and it is a study in contrast: Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and reared up for himself a pillar, which is in the king's dale: for he said, I have no son to keep my name in remembrance; and he called the pillar after his own name. The same ground, and two ways of seeking a name. Abram received a blessing from the priest of the most high God and gave away the spoil; Absalom built a monument to himself because he feared being forgotten. He died in a wood, was cast into a great pit, and had a heap of stones laid on him, while his father wept over the gate. Proverbs states the outcome the two dales illustrate: the memory of the just is blessed, but the name of the wicked shall rot.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a low place between hills; a vale or valley; in Scripture, the king's dale, where Melchizedek met Abram and where Absalom reared his pillar.
webster_full: DALE, n. A low place between hills; a vale or valley.
VALLEY, n. A hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains.
PILLAR, n. A kind of irregular column, round and insulated; a monument raised to preserve memory.
MONUMENT, n. Anything by which the memory of a person or of an event is preserved.
REMEMBRANCE, n. The retaining or having in mind an idea which had been present before.
scriptures: And the king of Sodom went out to meet him after his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer, and of the kings that were with him, at the valley of Shaveh, which is the king's dale.

Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and reared up for himself a pillar, which is in the king's dale: for he said, I have no son to keep my name in remembrance: and he called the pillar after his own name: and it is called unto this day, Absalom's place.

And the king was much moved, and went up to the chamber over the gate, and wept: and as he went, thus he said, O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!
Pro 10:7
The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot.
corruption_summary: The desire to be remembered is treated as a neutral good and pursued as legacy, when Scripture sets Absalom's self-named pillar against Abram's refusal of spoil and lets the outcomes speak.
corruption_paragraphs: Legacy is one of the few ambitions modern culture permits without qualification, and Absalom is its patron. I have no son to keep my name in remembrance: therefore a pillar, in the king's dale, called after his own name. Scripture records the pillar and then records the heap of stones in the wood that actually marked him, and the juxtaposition is the argument. The name a man makes for himself and the name he leaves are seldom the same object, and only one of them is in his hands.

Abram in the same valley shows the alternative and it is not modesty but worship. He tithes to Melchizedek, priest of the most high God, and swears he will take nothing from the king of Sodom lest that king should say, I have made Abram rich. He refuses a legacy from the wrong hand. The name he was given came from God: I will make thy name great, and thou shalt be a blessing. Proverbs draws the line the two dales draw: the memory of the just is blessed, but the name of the wicked shall rot.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'emeq (H6010), a valley or vale; Shaveh (H7740), plain or level; matstsebeth (H4678), a pillar or standing monument.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'emeq (H6010) — a vale, a valley, a low place; the king's dale.
Hebrew Shaveh (H7740) — level, plain; the valley of Shaveh, which is the king's dale.
Hebrew matstsebeth (H4678) — a standing pillar or monument; what Absalom reared for himself.
Hebrew zakar (H2142) — to remember, to mark; to keep my name in remembrance.
Hebrew shem (H8034) — a name, a reputation; he called the pillar after his own name.

“a pillar, which is in the king's dale” — where Absalom built for himself.
“The memory of the just is blessed” — the verdict on the two.

pos: n. (a great chasm; the fixed separation between the two states after death)
etymology: From Greek kolpos through Latin and French, a bosom or deep bay, and so a chasm. The Authorized Version uses it once, in the Lord's account of the rich man and Lazarus, of the great gulf fixed between Abraham's bosom and the place of torment.
biblical_def: Abraham's answer to the rich man contains three clauses and each closes a door. First, Son, remember that thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things, and likewise Lazarus evil things: but now he is comforted, and thou art tormented. Second, beside all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us, that would come from thence. Third, when the rich man asks that Lazarus be sent to his brothers, If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead. The gulf is fixed, and the word is emphatic: established, set fast. Nothing in the account suggests a temporary arrangement or a process of purification. The state is settled at death, and it is settled in both directions, for even those on the blessed side cannot cross. Hebrews states the same in plain doctrine: as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment. The passage is not a parable of social reversal only. It is the Lord's own description of what lies immediately on the other side of a man's last breath.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a deep place in the earth; an abyss; a chasm; in Scripture, the impassable separation fixed between the two states after death.
webster_full: GULF, n. A recess in the ocean from the general line of the shore; also, an abyss; a deep place in the earth.
GULF, n. A whirlpool; an absorbing eddy; anything insatiable.
ABYSS, n. A bottomless gulf; hence any deep, immeasurable space.
TORMENT, n. Extreme pain; anguish; the utmost degree of misery, either of body or mind.
IRREVERSIBLE, a. That cannot be reversed, recalled or annulled.
scriptures: And beside all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us, that would come from thence.
But Abraham said, Son, remember that thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things, and likewise Lazarus evil things: but now he is comforted, and thou art tormented.
And he said unto him, If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead.
Heb 9:27
And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:
corruption_summary: The fixed gulf is softened by purgatory, by post-mortem second chances, and by universalism, all of which require crossing a passage the Lord himself declares impassable in both directions.
corruption_paragraphs: Three doctrines founder on this verse. Purgatory requires a cleansing transit from one state toward the other; the text says they which would pass from hence to you cannot. Post-mortem evangelism requires a further offer after death; the text answers the request for a messenger with Moses and the prophets, meaning the word already given in this life is the means God has appointed and there is no other. Universalism requires the gulf to be eventually abolished; the Lord calls it fixed. The dictionary holds the historic Reformed position with the 1689 Confession: the souls of the righteous are received into paradise and the souls of the wicked cast into torments, and besides these two places for souls separated from their bodies, the Scripture acknowledgeth none.

The second corruption is gentler and commoner: reading the passage as being only about wealth and poverty, so that it becomes a parable of economic reversal with no doctrine of the afterlife in it. The economics are certainly there, and the rich man's five brothers are there, and the sin of feasting sumptuously every day while a beggar lay at the gate full of sores is named. But it is the Lord who supplies the geography, the conversation, and the verdict, and he supplies them as fact. If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead — a sentence that acquired terrible weight a few chapters later, when one did.

pos: n. (a breach in a wall; the place an intercessor is to stand)
etymology: From Old Norse gap, an opening or chasm. In the Authorized Version it is a breach in a city wall, and both prophetic uses turn it into a figure for intercession — the man who stands where the wall is broken.
biblical_def: And I sought for a man among them, that should make up the hedge, and stand in the gap before me for the land, that I should not destroy it: but I found none. The sentence comes at the end of a chapter cataloguing the sins of every class in Jerusalem — princes, priests, prophets, and people of the land — and it is the bleakest line in Ezekiel. God is not looking for an army. He is looking for one man to stand in a breach, and there is not one. The same prophet had already charged the false prophets with the failure: ye have not gone up into the gaps, neither made up the hedge for the house of Israel to stand in the battle in the day of the LORD. The image is a city wall with a hole in it, and the intercessor is the body that fills the hole. Psalm 106 names the man who once did it: had not Moses his chosen stood before him in the breach, to turn away his wrath, lest he should destroy them. This is why the New Testament's first instruction about public worship is what it is: I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): an opening or breach in a fence or wall; in Scripture, the breach where an intercessor stands between a people and the wrath they have earned.
webster_full: GAP, n. An opening in anything made by breaking or parting; a breach in a fence or wall.
BREACH, n. The act of breaking; a gap; an opening made by breaking, as in a wall.
HEDGE, n. A fence or inclosure formed of thorn bushes or other shrubs.
INTERCESSION, n. The act of interceding; mediation; interposition between parties at variance.
MEDIATOR, n. One that interposes between parties at variance for the purpose of reconciling them.
scriptures: And I sought for a man among them, that should make up the hedge, and stand in the gap before me for the land, that I should not destroy it: but I found none.
Eze 13:5
Ye have not gone up into the gaps, neither made up the hedge for the house of Israel to stand in the battle in the day of the LORD.
Therefore he said that he would destroy them, had not Moses his chosen stood before him in the breach, to turn away his wrath, lest he should destroy them.
I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men;
corruption_summary: Intercession is treated as a private devotional comfort for the one praying, when Scripture presents it as a public office performed on behalf of a people under judgment, and names its absence as a reason for ruin.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 22:30 sets prayer in a context most modern treatments avoid entirely. A nation is under sentence, the sentence is deserved, and God searches for a man to stand between the sentence and the people. Intercession here is dangerous, public, and costly: to stand in the gap is to occupy the place the enemy is coming through. Moses did it and offered to be blotted out of God's book instead of Israel; Abraham did it for Sodom, and pressed the number down from fifty to ten; Samuel called it sin to cease from praying for the people. The comforting devotional register has nothing to say to this and was never meant to.

The corruption also runs through the pulpit, and Ezekiel 13 names it there first. The prophets had not gone up into the gaps; they had daubed the wall with untempered morter and said peace where there was no peace. A ministry that will not name the breach cannot stand in it. Christ is the one who finally did: the Mediator between God and men, who ever liveth to make intercession for them, standing in a gap no other man could fill, and the church's praying is the small echo of his great intercession, commanded first of all.

Hebrew gader (H1447) — a wall, a fence, a hedge; make up the hedge.

Greek enteuxis (G1783) — an intercession, a petition; first of all, intercessions for all men.

“Moses his chosen stood before him in the breach” — the man who did.

pos: n. pl. (the upper air and clouds; the region of God's canopy and of falling righteousness)
etymology: From Old Norse sky, a cloud. The Authorized Version uses the plural five times, always of the cloud region rather than the starry heaven, and always in poetry.
biblical_def: The clouds poured out water: the skies sent out a sound: thine arrows also went abroad. Asaph is recounting the exodus, and the storm at the sea is described as the noise of God going through. The same picture stands in David's song of deliverance: he made darkness pavilions round about him, dark waters, and thick clouds of the skies. God is pictured as a King whose tent is built of storm, hidden in the very cloud from which he acts. Isaiah takes the same region and turns it toward salvation in one of the great verses of the Old Testament: Drop down, ye heavens, from above, and let the skies pour down righteousness: let the earth open, and let them bring forth salvation, and let righteousness spring up together; I the LORD have created it. Righteousness comes down as rain comes down. It is not grown in the ground and not manufactured by men; it falls, and then the earth brings forth salvation because it fell. And Jeremiah uses the skies to measure a judgment: Babylon's judgment reacheth unto heaven, and is lifted up even to the skies.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the aerial region which surrounds the earth; the apparent arch or vault of heaven; the clouds.
webster_full: SKY, n. The aerial region which surrounds the earth; the apparent arch or vault of heaven.
SKY, n. The heavens; the region of clouds and of the upper air.
FIRMAMENT, n. The region of the air; the sky or heavens.
CANOPY, n. A covering over a throne or over a bed; hence, a covering spread over the head.
RIGHTEOUSNESS, n. Purity of heart and rectitude of life; conformity of heart and life to the divine law.
scriptures: The clouds poured out water: the skies sent out a sound: thine arrows also went abroad.
And he made darkness pavilions round about him, dark waters, and thick clouds of the skies.
Isa 45:8

Drop down, ye heavens, from above, and let the skies pour down righteousness: let the earth open, and let them bring forth salvation, and let righteousness spring up together; I the LORD have created it.
Psa 97:6
The heavens declare his righteousness, and all the people see his glory.
corruption_summary: Righteousness is treated as a human achievement to be built upward, when Isaiah 45:8 has it falling from above as rain and the earth merely opening to receive what was sent.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 45:8 is a direction as much as a promise. The heavens drop down, the skies pour down righteousness, the earth opens, salvation is brought forth, and the verse closes the argument with a signature: I the LORD have created it. Every moral programme that proposes to generate righteousness from below — by education, by legislation, by sincerity, by self-improvement — is working against the grain of that verse. Righteousness is imputed before it is imparted, and it is imparted by the same God who imputed it. The earth's part is to open.

The second and more devotional use of the skies corrects a different error, which is the assumption that God's hiddenness is his absence. He made darkness his secret place; his pavilion round about him were dark waters and thick clouds of the skies. The cloud that conceals him is the tent he is acting from. Asaph in the same psalm says, thy way is in the sea, and thy path in the great waters, and thy footsteps are not known — and then, in the next breath, thou leddest thy people like a flock. Unseen and unfelt is not the same as absent, and the psalm is written to a man who could not sleep.
roots_summary: Hebrew shachaq (H7834), a cloud, the fine dust of the sky; 'ab (H5645), a thick cloud; tsedeq (H6664), righteousness.
roots_lines: Hebrew shachaq (H7834) — the clouds, the skies; from a root meaning to pulverize, and so fine dust.
Hebrew 'ab (H5645) — a dark, thick cloud; thick clouds of the skies.
Hebrew tsedeq (H6664) — rightness, righteousness; let the skies pour down righteousness.
Hebrew yesha' (H3468) — deliverance, salvation; let them bring forth salvation.
Hebrew nazal (H5140) — to flow, to trickle, to pour down; the verb of the falling.
usage: “the skies sent out a sound” — the storm at the sea in Asaph's psalm.
“let the skies pour down righteousness” — righteousness as rain, not as achievement.
“thick clouds of the skies” — the darkness God acts from.

pos: adj. (white or grey with age or frost)
etymology: Old English har, grey, venerable. The Authorized Version uses it of the frost on the wilderness ground the morning the manna came, and of the grey head of an old man.
biblical_def: Two pictures share one word. The first is the morning of the manna: when the dew that lay was gone up, behold, upon the face of the wilderness there lay a small round thing, as small as the hoar frost on the ground. The bread of heaven arrived looking like frost, and had to be gathered every morning, and bred worms if hoarded. The second is age. David charges Solomon concerning Joab, let not his hoar head go down to the grave in peace, and concerning Shimei, his hoar head bring thou down to the grave with blood — grey hair is no immunity from justice. Yet the same greyness is honoured where it is honourable: the hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness, which is a conditional crown and says so. The verse the dictionary keeps above all is Isaiah's, where God takes the hoar head to himself: and even to your old age I am he; and even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you. The God who made a man in the womb undertakes to carry him out of the world.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): white; grey with age; white with frost; hence, venerable, applied to age.
webster_full: HOAR, a. White; as hoar frost; hoary.
HOAR, a. White or grey with age; as hoar hairs.
HOARY, a. White or whitish; white or grey with age; hence, venerable.
FROST, n. A fluid congealed by cold; also, the white particles of dew congealed on the ground.
AGE, n. The whole duration of a being, whether animal or vegetable; a period of life.
scriptures: Isa 46:4
And even to your old age I am he; and even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you.
And when the dew that lay was gone up, behold, upon the face of the wilderness there lay a small round thing, as small as the hoar frost on the ground.
The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness.
Do therefore according to thy wisdom, and let not his hoar head go down to the grave in peace.
corruption_summary: Age is treated as decline to be delayed and hidden, and the old as a class to be managed; Scripture makes grey hair an honour where righteousness earned it, refuses it as a shelter from justice, and makes God himself the one who carries a man to the end.
corruption_paragraphs: A culture organised around youth has two settled opinions about old age, that it is a medical problem and that it is an embarrassment, and Isaiah 46:4 contradicts both. The verse is God speaking against the idols of Babylon, which have to be carried on beasts and are a burden to the weary. God's claim is the opposite: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you. The idol is freight; the LORD is the porter. And the span he commits to is the whole of it, from the belly to hoar hairs, which is the strongest statement in the Old Testament of preserving grace over a lifetime.

Proverbs supplies the balance so that the honour due to age is not sentimental. The hoary head is a crown of glory — if it be found in the way of righteousness. And David's charge about Joab shows the other edge: a long life of bloodshed does not buy a peaceful grave. The dictionary therefore honours the aged as the fifth commandment requires, refuses the flattery that treats years alone as wisdom, and holds out the promise to those growing old in Christ that the carrying is God's work and not theirs.

pos: n. (in ferry boat, a boat for carrying over a river)
etymology: Old English ferian, to carry or convey. The Authorized Version uses it once, in the phrase a ferry boat, at the crossing of Jordan when David returned to Jerusalem after Absalom's rebellion.
biblical_def: And there went over a ferry boat to carry over the king's household, and to do what he thought good. And Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king, as he was come over Jordan. The detail matters because of who is lying in the mud at the landing. Shimei is the man who had cursed David as he fled, casting stones and dust and calling him a bloody man, and David had refused to let Abishai take his head: let him curse, because the LORD hath said unto him, Curse David. Now the king is coming back with the kingdom, and Shimei is the first man over the river. Abishai says again, shall not Shimei be put to death for this, that he cursed the LORD's anointed? David answers, shall there any man be put to death this day in Israel? and says to Shimei, Thou shalt not die. And the king sware unto him. The ferry boat crossing is therefore one of the great scenes of restraint in the Old Testament, and the New Testament command rests on the same ground David gave for it: avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a boat or small vessel in which passengers are conveyed over a river; also the place of crossing.
webster_full: FERRY, v.t. To carry or transport over a river or other water in a boat.
FERRY, n. A boat or small vessel in which passengers and goods are conveyed over rivers.
FERRYBOAT, n. A boat for conveying passengers over rivers or other narrow waters.
VENGEANCE, n. The infliction of pain on another in return for an injury or offense.
CLEMENCY, n. Mildness; softness; mercy; disposition to treat with lenity.
scriptures: And there went over a ferry boat to carry over the king's household, and to do what he thought good. And Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king, as he was come over Jordan;
Therefore the king said unto Shimei, Thou shalt not die. And the king sware unto him.
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
Mat 5:44
But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;
corruption_summary: Forgiveness is presented as the denial that any wrong was done, so that mercy requires pretending; David forgives Shimei while naming exactly what Shimei did, and leaves the reckoning with God.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic account of forgiveness makes it an inward exercise in releasing one's own resentment, and it tends to require that the offence be minimised for the exercise to work. Scripture does the opposite. The record of Shimei's cursing is preserved in detail, Abishai's demand for justice is recorded without rebuke of its logic, and David's oath is given with full knowledge of the crime. Forgiveness in the Bible is a transaction about a real debt, which is why it costs something and why it can be sworn to.

The second half of the truth is that David's clemency was not an acquittal before God. He charged Solomon at the end of his life to deal with Joab and with Shimei according to wisdom, and Shimei died years later for breaking a further oath he had sworn himself. The dictionary therefore distinguishes personal forgiveness, which is commanded of every Christian, from the magistrate's duty to punish evildoers, which is his office under God. Romans 12 forbids private vengeance and Romans 13 arms the magistrate, and they are the same paragraph.

pos: n. pl. (marshes; low wet ground where the reed grows)
etymology: Old English fenn, mud or marsh. The Authorized Version uses the plural once, in the LORD's description of behemoth, who lies under the shady trees in the covert of the reed and the fens.
biblical_def: He lieth under the shady trees, in the covert of the reed, and fens. The subject is behemoth, and the whole passage is deliberately unhurried. Behold now behemoth, which I made with thee; he eateth grass as an ox; his strength is in his loins, and his force is in the navel of his belly; he moveth his tail like a cedar; his bones are as strong pieces of brass. And then this: he lies down in the marsh, in the shade, among the reeds, entirely at ease. The LORD is showing Job a creature of enormous power that spends its days resting in a swamp, and the sentence that frames the whole exhibit is the one about origin — which I made with thee. Behemoth and Job came from the same hand. Leviathan follows immediately, and the argument reaches its point there: none is so fierce that dare stir him up: who then is able to stand before me? If a man will not provoke a beast, what is he doing arraigning the beast's Maker? Job's reply is the right one and the dictionary keeps it: I know that thou canst do every thing, and that no thought can be withholden from thee.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): low land overflowed, or covered wholly or partially with water, but producing sedge, coarse grasses or reeds; a moor or marsh.
webster_full: FEN, n. Low land overflowed, or covered wholly or partially with water; a moor; a marsh; a bog.
MARSH, n. A tract of low land, usually or occasionally covered with water.
REED, n. The common name of many aquatic plants; most of them large grasses.
COVERT, n. A shelter; a defense; a thicket; a hiding place.
BEHEMOTH, n. Authors are divided in opinion as to the animal intended in Scripture by this name.
scriptures: He lieth under the shady trees, in the covert of the reed, and fens.
Behold now behemoth, which I made with thee; he eateth grass as an ox.
None is so fierce that dare stir him up: who then is able to stand before me?
Job 42:2
I know that thou canst do every thing, and that no thought can be withholden from thee.
corruption_summary: Behemoth and leviathan are explained away as myth or as poetic exaggeration, which removes the whole force of the LORD's argument; the text presents them as creatures God made, exhibited to a man who had been questioning his government.
corruption_paragraphs: The historical-critical habit of treating the great beasts of Job 40 and 41 as borrowed mythological monsters empties the passage of its function. The argument only works if these are creatures — things God actually made and actually sustains, lying in actual fens, which Job can neither capture nor comprehend. Which I made with thee is the hinge of the whole speech, setting the man and the beast side by side as fellow creatures of one Maker. A myth proves nothing about Job's competence to judge the world; a living animal he cannot stir up proves a great deal.

The corresponding error among believers is to make these chapters a puzzle about zoology and miss what they are for. God is not identifying a species; he is finishing an argument that began with the foundations of the earth and ends with a question that leaves no room: who then is able to stand before me? Job's answer is not an explanation received but a Person seen, and the dictionary counts that the model for every sufferer who has been told to be quiet: I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear, but now mine eye seeth thee.
